rationale: Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported trait/phenotyping (M13 Other arthritis), same EFO mapping (arthritis), same training cohort (UKB), identical training/validation sizes and EUR-only DEV/EVAL, and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only OR reported; covariates unknown). With metrics otherwise indistinguishable, the main differentiator is the available PRS effect size: PGS004547 reports a higher per-SD OR (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), indicating stronger PRS signal in the same validation context. Method_name also favors PGS004547 structurally (meta/ensemble-style RFDiseasemetaPRS vs single-score LDpred2), but the decision is primarily supported by the stronger reported OR.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment to the target (trait_efo=alcohol dependence; trait_reported/phenotyping_reported=Alcohol use disorder) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so selection rests on effect-size evidence and structural signals. PGS002738 shows a stronger reported discrimination proxy (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51]) than PGS002739 (1.76 [1.32–2.34]) and uses a genome-wide PRS-CS with far broader variant coverage (326,000 vs 858), which is generally favorable for a polygenic trait when metrics are otherwise missing. PGS002739’s main advantage is AFR-only evaluation ancestry, but it is paired with a much sparser gene-based score and slightly weaker OR evidence. With covariates unknown for both, PGS002738 is better-supported overall.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.539) and PGS-only R² (0.00291) with basic covariates listed, allowing a clean sanity check against the arthritis heritability ceiling and showing the PRS contribution is small but quantified. It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) rather than EUR-only. In contrast, PGS004547 has a more specific reported endpoint (“M13 Other arthritis”) and a genome-wide variant count, but it provides no AUROC/R² (only an OR=1.26, which is weak-to-moderate) and has unknown covariates, making its predictive performance and comparability much less verifiable from the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target trait well (same trait_reported/trait_efo). However, PGS000753 uses a prevalent AAA endpoint and provides only an OR=1.37 (moderate) with no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 reported, and it is a very sparse P+T score (29 variants). PGS003973 is from a large disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis context and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is a stronger structural signal when PRS-only metrics are absent for both. Although PGS003973 reports only a full-model C-index (0.882) that is not PRS-comparable, its covariates are basic (age/age^2/sex) and the overall evidence package (multi-cohort development + genome-wide model) is stronger than the sparse, prevalent-endpoint PGS000753.

PGS001267 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait (ankylosing spondylitis) with a direct disease case-control phenotype (“Ankylosing spondylitis” / phenotyping_reported “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly time-to-event (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)” / phenotyping_reported “TTE ankylosing spondylitis”), which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS001268 shows slightly higher PRS-comparable metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346 vs 0.7265; PGS-only R2 0.1023 vs 0.0988), both are near-clones from the same pan-trait UKB framework paper with identical training/validation sizes, ancestries, variant count, and covariates, so the small metric edge is weak evidence compared with the endpoint mismatch. Both R2 values are below the heritability ceiling, so heritability does not differentiate them.

PGS005254 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): its trait_reported and trait_efo are directly aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is labeled as “Mean pressure gradient” with a broader/mixed trait_efo (“aortic stenosis, aortic measurement”), making it more measurement/proxy-oriented despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported (incident aortic stenosis). Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, PRS-CS, EUR-only dev/eval, identical covariates, same validation N, no PRS-only AUC/R2), so the tie-breakers are endpoint fidelity and available effect size; PGS005254 also shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53).

Both candidates are near-clones for the target trait (identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported = abdominal aortic aneurysm), same method (PRS-CS), same variant count (1,118,997), and same evaluation ancestry (EUR only), so endpoint fidelity and structural signals do not differentiate. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics), so performance evidence is not cleanly comparable as PRS. Given that, the only meaningful visible edge is that PGS003973 reports a time-to-event style discrimination metric (C-index 0.882 with CI) with explicitly basic covariates (age, age^2, sex), whereas PGS003972 has a much lower full-model AUROC (0.69) with covariates listed as unknown. Because full-model metrics are discounted and covariate differences make them hard to compare, confidence is low, but PGS003973 has the cleaner disclosed covariate set and stronger reported discrimination.

PGS001135 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC (0.539) and PGS-only R² (0.00291), allowing a clean comparison and a heritability-ceiling sanity check, whereas PGS004477 provides no AUROC/R² at all (only an OR=1.20) and has unknown covariates, making its predictive performance and comparability hard to judge. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (both map to EFO arthritis), but PGS004477’s reported phenotype is a narrower ICD10-style category (“M13 Other arthritis”) while PGS001135 targets broader “Arthritis (nos)” consistent with the generic target. Although PGS001135 comes from a known pan-trait UKB framework paper (a negative), the absence of comparable performance metrics for PGS004477 leaves PGS001135 as the more evidentially supported choice overall.

PGS004913 is the better-supported match for alcoholic liver cirrhosis because its endpoint fidelity is cleaner (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both explicitly “Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis”), whereas PGS001777 has a phenotyping mismatch/restriction (“Cirrhosis (males)”) and unclear covariates (“Unknown”). Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS001777’s reported AUROC=0.671 is a full-model metric and not a comparable PRS metric; in that setting, PGS004913’s reported R²=0.029 and OR (top vs bottom deciles)=4.4 provide at least some quantification alongside clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, 10 PCs). Structurally, PGS004913 also uses more variants (20 vs 3) and has explicit training (n=3,037) with a larger validation (n=3,360 vs 1,390), giving a more complete and transparent evidence package than PGS001777.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target (trait_efo = alcoholic liver cirrhosis). However, PGS001777 is more endpoint-faithful in study intent (publication explicitly about predicting alcohol-related cirrhosis in drinkers) and provides stronger PRS signal evidence via a large stratification effect (OR top 20% vs bottom 20% = 6.18) despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2. PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics framework paper (less disease-focused), reports only a full-model C-index (0.711) with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) but shows only modest genetic effect size (HR 1.18), and its full-model metric is not PRS-comparable. With no PRS-only metrics for either, the stronger effect-size evidence and disease-focused endpoint context favor PGS001777 over PGS000704.

Both candidates match the target trait well at the concept level (trait_reported/trait_efo = asthma). However, PGS001782 provides a clearly PRS-comparable performance metric (Nagelkerke R2 with covariates regressed out / pgs_only_r2 = 0.048844) plus an AUROC (0.659) with explicitly basic covariates (sex, age, 20 PCs), and its PRS-only R2 is below the asthma heritability ceiling (h2_obs ~0.0077; liability ~0.1515), making it interpretable. In contrast, PGS002727 is pediatric-asthma specific (endpoint narrower than generic asthma) and reports only full-model metrics (AUROC 0.66, R2 0.04) with covariates listed as unknown, so its discrimination evidence is less clean/comparable despite a supportive OR=1.57 and broader multi-ancestry evaluation. Given the stronger PRS-only metric clarity and cleaner covariate disclosure, PGS001782 is better supported on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target trait well (AAA; EFO aligned). However, PGS003972 is built with a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) and ~1.1M variants from a large multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis context, which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than PGS000753’s very sparse P+T score with 29 variants. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS003972’s AUROC=0.69 is full-model and thus not PRS-comparable, but PGS000753 provides only an OR per SD (1.37, moderate) with no AUC/R2. Covariates are basic/clean for PGS000753 (age/sex/PCs) while PGS003972 has unknown covariates (a confidence penalty), yet there is no explicit clinical-risk packaging or biomarker leakage shown for either. Overall, the stronger methodological/variant-coverage and disease-focused multi-cohort development support PGS003972 over the sparse 29-variant PGS000753.

PGS002738 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint fidelity is direct: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both Alcohol use disorder and trait_efo maps exactly to alcohol dependence. In contrast, PGS000201 is centered on “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo mapped to an alcohol dependence measurement, making the target alignment more indirect despite its phenotyping_reported referencing DSM-5 AUD criteria count. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on comparable effect evidence: PGS002738 shows a stronger risk stratification signal (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96, 95% CI 1.54–2.51) whereas PGS000201 only provides a small incremental ΔR²=0.01192 (and a beta on a transformed count outcome), which is harder to interpret as disease-risk discrimination. Covariates are unknown for PGS002738 (confidence penalty), but PGS000201’s covariates are basic and not leakage-heavy; overall the stronger endpoint match plus clearer, larger effect-size evidence favors PGS002738.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo are aortic stenosis; both use incident aortic stenosis phenotyping; both DEV/EVAL EUR only) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on effect-size evidence and covariate cleanliness rather than full-model metrics. PGS005254 has a much cleaner, PRS-comparable evaluation setup (covariates limited to age/age^2/sex/PCs) and reports an HR per SD of 1.64 with CI (1.50–1.78), which is interpretable as PRS signal. PGS005252 reports a higher HR (1.92) but without CI and its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index 0.87 alongside a very heavy comorbidity/risk-factor covariate set (T2D, HTN, CAD, hyperlipidemia, BMI, smoking, renal failure), making that performance evidence likely covariate-driven and less comparable to standalone PRS quality. Training/validation sizes differ but are weak tie-breakers here.

PGS001344 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.64568 and PGS-only R2=0.05973 (no covariates), which can be sanity-checked against asthma liability h2 (~0.15) and are clearly interpretable as PRS signal. In contrast, PGS002727 lacks any PGS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC=0.66 and R2=0.04), and per policy the full-model AUROC cannot substitute for PRS-only discrimination, making its performance evidence less clean despite a strong OR=1.57 and a disease-focused pediatric-asthma context. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (asthma), but PGS002727 is pediatric-specific (potentially narrower than generic asthma), while PGS001344 uses a direct doctor-diagnosed asthma phenotype with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/array) and provides cleaner comparable metrics.

PGS001268 is better supported on PRS-comparable performance: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.7346 and PGS-only R²=0.10232 (with CIs for AUROC), whereas PGS002089 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919) and has no PGS-only AUC/R², making its predictive strength harder to assess. Endpoint fidelity is slightly cleaner for PGS002089 (direct ankylosing spondylitis) versus PGS001268’s time-to-event (TTE) phenotype, but this mismatch is modest and outweighed here by the much clearer PRS-only metrics in PGS001268. Covariates are basic in both (age/sex/PCs/array-type/deprivation), with no strong leakage signals. Overall, PGS001268 has the stronger visible evidence package for ankylosing spondylitis risk prediction despite the TTE framing.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is directly aligned across fields (trait_reported="Alcohol use disorder", trait_efo="alcohol dependence", phenotyping_reported="Alcohol use disorder"), whereas PGS000201 is more indirect (trait_reported="Problematic alcohol use" and trait_efo="alcohol dependence measurement"), even though its phenotyping is AUD DSM-5 criteria count. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on endpoint fidelity and available effect evidence: PGS002739 provides a clear case-control discrimination signal (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76), while PGS000201 reports only a small incremental ΔR² (0.01192) plus a beta on a transformed count outcome, which is harder to compare to dependence risk. Covariates are explicitly basic/clean for PGS000201 but unknown for PGS002739; this lowers confidence, but not enough to outweigh PGS002739’s tighter alcohol-dependence mapping and more interpretable risk stratification metric.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ankylosing spondylitis) and use only basic covariates (no obvious clinical-risk packaging). PGS001267 is better supported because it reports explicit PRS-comparable performance metrics in Europeans (PGS-only AUROC=0.7265; PGS-only R²=0.0988), enabling a direct PRS-quality comparison and a heritability sanity check, whereas PGS002089 provides only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.0919) and has no PGS-only AUROC/R². Although PGS002089 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants (22,026) and has some multi-ancestry evaluation, the lack of standard PRS-only discrimination metrics makes its evidence weaker on the visible fields than PGS001267’s clearly reported PGS-only AUROC/R².

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): its trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are directly aligned to incident aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is primarily reported as a valve-function quantitative trait (“Mean pressure gradient”) with a broader/mixed trait_efo (“aortic stenosis, aortic measurement”), making endpoint fidelity weaker. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on available effect-size and design signals; PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), suggesting stronger PRS discrimination. Although PGS005252’s reported C-index=0.87 is full-model and likely covariate-inflated (it includes many clinical covariates), it still provides some supportive evidence; PGS005255 has no discrimination metric beyond HR. Both are EUR-only dev/eval; PGS005252 also has larger validation N (446,895 vs 244,450), a weak but supportive tie-break. Confidence is Moderate because PGS005252’s heavy covariate set makes its full-model metric non-comparable, and both lack clean PRS-only performance metrics.

PGS004913 is better supported for the specific target of alcoholic liver cirrhosis because it is explicitly disease-focused and endpoint-faithful (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Alcohol-associated liver cirrhosis”) and provides PRS-relevant effect evidence (OR top vs bottom deciles = 4.4) with only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs). In contrast, PGS000704 comes from a broad biomarker genetics framework paper and the only discrimination metric shown is a full-model C-index (0.711) rather than a PRS-only metric, making its apparent performance less comparable for PRS quality; its per-SD HR (1.18) also suggests weaker PRS signal. Both are EFO-aligned and largely EUR-evaluated, so the decision hinges on stronger endpoint focus and more compelling PRS effect evidence for PGS004913.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUC/C-index is not directly comparable as a PRS metric. PGS005168’s reported discrimination is heavily confounded by explicit clinical risk-calculator packaging (covariates include CHARGE-AF), which is a strong negative comparability signal; its high C-index (0.8718) is therefore likely covariate-driven and discounted. PGS005313 uses only basic covariates (age, sex), avoiding that leakage, and provides a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.82) plus a genome-wide cross-ancestry construction (PRS-CSx, 1.27M variants) with multi-ancestry evaluation context. Given cleaner covariates and stronger standalone genetic signal evidence, PGS005313 is better-supported despite the lower full-model AUROC.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation). However, PGS005168’s only discrimination metric shown is a full-model C-index 0.8718 and it explicitly includes the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator in covariates, which is strong risk-wrapper packaging and makes the reported performance largely non-comparable to standalone PRS quality. PGS002814 also reports only full-model metrics (AUROC 0.74; pseudo-R2 0.14), but its covariates are basic (age, sex, PCs) without a named clinical calculator, and it provides a strong PRS effect size (OR≈1.94 per SD). Despite being evaluated only in East Asians, the cleaner covariate setup and strong effect-size evidence make PGS002814 better-supported on the visible fields than the CHARGE-AF-packaged PGS005168.

PGS004587 is better aligned to the target trait as a general atopic eczema/atopic dermatitis endpoint (trait_reported: "Atopic dermatitis"; phenotyping_reported: "Incident atopic dermatitis"), whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype ("Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis") and thus is less faithful to generic atopic eczema risk. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS001773’s very high AUROC=0.93 and R²=0.49 are full-model metrics (and include parental ethnicity covariates), so they are not comparable PRS evidence and are also implausibly high relative to the eczema heritability ceiling, reducing their interpretability. PGS004587 at least reports a PRS-stratified HR (1.153 high vs low) in a large EUR evaluation (n=337,910) with non-clinical covariates, making it the cleaner, more on-target choice despite sparse-variant construction.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_efo=atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported=incident atopic dermatitis) and have identical covariates and validation ancestry/size (EUR; n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics largely non-differentiating, structural/model-quality signals dominate: PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is generally better suited to a polygenic trait like atopic eczema than PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNP score. The HR separation is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR 1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587’s listed multi-cohort training sources are supportive but not enough to outweigh the much stronger genome-wide construction and effect size evidence in PGS002755 given otherwise near-identical endpoint and evaluation context.

PGS001263 is the better match to the target trait (atrial flutter) because its trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all specifically “Atrial flutter,” whereas PGS001339 is explicitly a combined and time-to-event endpoint (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter (time-to-event)” / “TTE atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is a phenotype/endpoint mismatch for a generic atrial flutter target. On PRS-comparable metrics they are near-identical, but PGS001263 is slightly higher (PGS-only AUROC 0.61716 and R2 0.02517 vs 0.613 and 0.02447 for PGS001339), with similarly basic covariates and the same training/validation sizes; thus endpoint fidelity breaks the tie in favor of PGS001263.

PGS001263 is a direct endpoint match to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Atrial flutter”) and it reports clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R²=0.025), which can be sanity-checked against the provided heritability ceiling and interpreted without substituting full-model AUROC. In contrast, PGS002050 targets a broader combined phenotype (“Atrial fibrillation and flutter”) rather than atrial flutter specifically, and it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only partial correlation is provided), making its PRS discrimination evidence less directly comparable for this head-to-head despite larger variant count and training N.

PGS001782 is better supported structurally for asthma PRS quality: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS-auto) with very large variant coverage (884,043) and is developed in a broad multi-biobank/global context (many training/development cohorts; multi-ancestry GWAS), which is generally more robust than sparse pan-trait UKB framework scores. Although PGS001344 reports explicit PRS-only AUROC/R2 (PGS AUROC 0.6457; PGS R2 0.0597) and has larger validation n, it comes from the known pan-trait “813 traits” snpnet framework with a very sparse model (6,139 variants) and single-biobank development (UKB), a pattern associated with weaker external generalization. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (doctor-diagnosed asthma vs generic asthma), and both use only basic covariates; the performance edge for PGS001344 is modest and not enough to outweigh the framework/sparsity penalty given PGS001782’s comparable PRS-only R2 evidence (covariates-regressed-out R2=0.0488) and stronger cross-cohort development.

PGS002032 is the cleaner match to the target concept (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both specifically “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” mapped to bilirubin metabolism disease) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with many variants (LDpred2; 19,768 SNPs), with basic covariates and explicit multi-ancestry evaluation listed. PGS000924 has a broader, partially off-target endpoint (“Disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism” time-to-event; dual EFO mapping) and comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (snpnet; only 5 variants), which is a generalization risk despite reporting PRS-only AUROC/R². Confidence is low because PGS002032 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² (only partial-r), while PGS000924 provides explicit PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones: identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (basal cell carcinoma), same publication, same EUR-only ancestry distribution, same training cohort (MGI) and training N (11,734), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), same validation N (11,322), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC ~0.632, which is not PRS-comparable). With endpoint fidelity and comparability essentially identical, the only visible differentiator is slightly stronger reported performance/effect evidence for PGS000454: marginally higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0489 vs 0.0487) and higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.79 vs 3.61) while AUROC CIs are identical. Differences are tiny, so confidence is low, but PGS000454 has the slight edge.

PGS002755 is the better-supported standalone PRS for the target atopic eczema because it matches the generic disease concept (trait_efo atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported incident atopic dermatitis) without restricting to a severity subtype, and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic trait than PGS001773’s 25-variant GWAS-hit score. PGS001773’s only reported discrimination (AUROC=0.93, R²=0.49) appears to be full-model (not PGS-only) and is paired with family/ethnicity covariates, making it non-comparable and potentially covariate-driven; the R² is also implausibly high relative to the provided eczema heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.071), further discounting it. Although PGS002755 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² and reports only a modest HR (1.249 high vs low PRS), its endpoint is broader and its performance evidence is not inflated by an obviously non-PRS metric, making it the more reliable choice overall.

Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Disorders of bilirubin excretion” mapped to the same EFO), identical covariates, identical training cohort and size (UKB n=391,124), identical ancestry distribution, and essentially identical PRS-comparable performance evidence (partial-r=0.0716 with overlapping CIs). With metrics and phenotype alignment tied, the main differentiator is structural: PGS002032 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (19,768 variants) versus PGS001824’s very sparse penalized regression score (22 variants). Given the same study family and indistinguishable observed partial-r, the higher-coverage shrinkage model is better-supported as a general-purpose PRS for this trait.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same method (GWAS Hits), same EUR-only ancestry for GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sample sizes, and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC differences are not strong PRS-comparable evidence. With endpoints and design effectively identical, PGS000452 has a marginally higher full-model AUROC (0.632 vs 0.630) and higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0487 vs 0.0456), while PGS000456’s slightly higher top-1% OR does not outweigh the overall near-tie. Hence PGS000452 wins on the small but more consistently better discrimination metrics, with low confidence due to minimal separability.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly “Bipolar disorder/bipolar disorder,” whereas PGS002787 targets the narrower subtype “Type 1 bipolar disorder/bipolar I disorder.” Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, SDPR method, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, same basic covariates age+PCs1-3, no PGS-only AUC/R2, and only tiny partial R² values), so the slightly higher partial R² in PGS002787 is not a meaningful differentiator—especially given both have endpoint-fidelity issues in phenotyping_reported that are not direct bipolar diagnosis endpoints. Hence the decision rests mainly on concept alignment, favoring PGS002786.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Given that, structural and transportability signals dominate: PGS005313 uses a genome-wide shrinkage cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with ~1.27M variants and is evaluated across multiple ancestries, with a strong per-SD OR (1.82) under basic covariates (age, sex). PGS002814 is a sparse P+T score with only 4,520 variants and evaluation limited to East Asian; while it reports a full-model AUROC (0.74) and Nagelkerke R2 (0.14), these are not PRS-only and the R2 magnitude is hard to interpret for a P+T model without clearer PRS-only context. Overall, PGS005313 has stronger methodological/variant-coverage support and broader evaluation, making it the better-supported choice on the visible fields.

PGS000924 has clearly reported PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.88697 and PGS-only R²=0.21843) on a European validation record, whereas PGS001824 reports no PRS-only AUC/R² (only a modest partial correlation partial-r=0.0716), making its predictive support much weaker on the visible fields. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS000924 is a broader composite/time-to-event phenotype (“TTE disorders of porphyrin and bilirubin metabolism”) while PGS001824 is more directly aligned (“Disorders of bilirubin excretion”); however, that phenotype advantage for PGS001824 is outweighed by the much stronger and cleaner PRS-only metric evidence in PGS000924. Confidence is moderated because PGS000924’s PGS-only R² (0.218) exceeds the provided local heritability ceiling estimate (h2_obs≈0.089), suggesting possible scale/definition mismatch, but it still provides substantially more explicit PRS-only performance evidence than PGS001824.

Both candidates are near-clones in study context (same publication, SDPR method, PGC training cohort, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, basic covariates age+PCs1-3) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²; both only show a small partial R² (full-model/partial) that is not clearly PRS-comparable. Endpoint fidelity to the target trait “bipolar disorder” is slightly better for PGS002787 because its mapped trait is bipolar I disorder (Type 1), which is closer to the umbrella bipolar disorder concept than PGS002788’s bipolar II disorder (Type 2), while both have noisy/non-diagnostic phenotyping_reported fields. PGS002788 has a marginally higher partial R² and slightly larger validation N, but these differences are weak and likely noise given non-PRS-only metrics and mismatched phenotyping labels, so the subtype-to-target alignment breaks the tie in favor of PGS002787.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002788 targets the subtype bipolar II disorder. Both candidates are otherwise near-clones (same publication, SDPR method, PGC training cohort, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, same covariates age+PCs1-3, same validation n=2,524) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; both only show small partial R² values from non-disease phenotyping contexts. Although PGS002788 has a slightly higher partial R² (0.00307 vs 0.00251), the endpoint fidelity advantage of PGS002786 to the requested bipolar disorder outweighs this minor, non-PRS-comparable metric difference.

Both candidates target the correct endpoint family (trait_efo includes atrial flutter; phenotyping_reported is atrial fibrillation and flutter). However, PGS001339 provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.613 and PGS-only R2=0.02447), which can be sanity-checked against the atrial flutter h2_obs ceiling (~0.0157) and interpreted directly as PRS signal, whereas PGS002050 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2 entirely and reports only a partial correlation (partial-r=0.1034), making cross-model PRS discrimination support weaker/less standard. Although PGS002050 has a larger variant set and training N, the missing PRS-comparable metrics reduce evidentiary support versus PGS001339’s explicit PGS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (same EFO; phenotyping_reported is a direct Dupuytren/palmar fascia contracture diagnosis in both). Both candidates have essentially identical endpoint fidelity for Hashimoto’s thyroiditis (trait_efo matches; phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are the same: lymphocytic thyroiditis), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown for both—so phenotype/transportability do not differentiate. Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_efo Hashimoto's thyroiditis; phenotyping_reported lymphocytic thyroiditis), come from the same publication family, and have the same evaluation ancestry mix and validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown for both—so endpoint fidelity and transportability are essentially tied. Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Hodgkin's disease; trait_efo: Hodgkins lymphoma), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (so full-model AUROC is only weakly informative). Both candidates have identical endpoint fidelity to hodgkins lymphoma (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Hodgkin's disease”), identical ancestry context (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), same training cohort (MGI) and training/validation sizes (n=736 train; n=775 eval), and similarly clean/basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4). Both candidates target the same endpoint with identical trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Hodgkin's disease / Hodgkins lymphoma), same EUR-only ancestry across GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and training n=736, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=775). Both candidates match the target concept well (trait_reported/trait_efo are identical), but PGS002763 has cleaner endpoint fidelity: phenotyping_reported is generic “Hip osteoarthritis” versus PGS004882’s “Incident hip osteoarthritis,” which is a narrower time-to-event framing for a generic disease target. PGS005083 is the better-supported heart-failure PRS on the visible fields because it provides stronger PRS-specific evidence via effect size (OR per SD 1.455, close to the ≥1.5 “strong” guideline) with only basic covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs) and a directly aligned diagnosis endpoint (CHF PheCode 428.1; EFO congestive heart failure). Overall, the disease-focused multi-cohort design plus strong effect size for the dominant subtype outweighs the framework score’s modest PRS-only AUROC/R2.

Both candidates match the target trait well (trait_reported/trait_efo are heart failure), but PGS005097 is supported by a more disease-focused, heart-failure–specific study context (Nat Genet paper on HF genetic architecture; includes HERMES and multiple HF-relevant biobanks) and uses a cross-ancestry method (PRS-CSx) with multi-ancestry GWAS inputs and some non-EUR evaluation (European plus African unspecified), which is a positive transportability signal versus PGS001790 coming from a known portability/framework-style paper (“Global Biobank analyses…”). Confidence is moderate because PGS001790’s explicit PGS-only R2 is a meaningful advantage and PGS005097 lacks PRS-only performance reporting.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and use only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), so phenotype fidelity and leakage risk are similar. PGS004253 comes from a disease-focused UC study context and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,575) plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.84), which is meaningful PRS evidence even though it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only a full-model AUROC 0.66 that cannot be treated as PRS-only). Given the framework penalty and sparsity concerns for PGS001306 versus the stronger disease-focused, genome-wide PRS signal in PGS004253, PGS004253 is better-supported overall.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait_reported/trait_efo (bladder cancer / urinary bladder carcinoma), same phenotyping_reported (Cancer of bladder), same method (GWAS Hits) with the same 13 variants, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same publication and covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so the full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS-comparable differentiator). PGS000610 has a trivially higher full-model AUROC (0.572 vs 0.567) and pseudo-R² (0.013 vs 0.0114), but these small differences are likely noise given identical covariate structure and lack of PRS-only metrics; meanwhile PGS000611 shows stronger tail separation (OR top 1% vs rest 2.66 vs 1.47) and larger validation sample size (13,530 vs 7,622). With no PRS-only metrics available, I slightly prefer PGS000611 on the stronger extreme-risk OR and broader evaluation support, but the decision is close.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported (Urinary calculus/urolithiasis), same UKB-only training (n=391,124), same covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=19,913), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiators are (1) comparable performance signal and (2) structural method/coverage: PGS002075 has higher partial correlation (partial-r 0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach with far more variants (731,196 vs 5,599), which is a positive structural signal when other fields are effectively identical. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available, these modest but consistent advantages favor PGS002075.

PGS001864 is the better match to the target trait urolithiasis on endpoint fidelity: its trait_efo is exactly urolithiasis and phenotyping_reported/trait_reported are a direct diagnosis-style “Urinary calculus,” whereas PGS001250 is a narrower/higher-packaged endpoint (“Calculus of kidney and ureter (time-to-event)”) with trait_efo mapped to nephrolithiasis/ureterolithiasis rather than the umbrella urolithiasis. Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592) and PGS001864 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r=0.0323), the metric advantage is modest and comes from a known pan-trait sparse UKB framework paper, while PGS001864 comes from a portability evaluation with broader multi-ancestry evaluation and a much larger variant set (5599 vs 341), supporting a more polygenic capture. Confidence is low because PGS001864’s missing PRS-comparable AUC/R2 prevents a direct performance comparison against PGS001250’s explicit PRS-only metrics.

PGS002075 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait urolithiasis because its endpoint is a direct disease-status phenotype (“Urinary calculus” mapped to urolithiasis) rather than the more packaging-prone time-to-event formulation in PGS001250 (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”), which domain guidance flags as a weaker endpoint match for a generic disease target when alternatives exist. Although PGS001250 reports explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.5668; PGS R2 0.00592), it comes from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very small variant set (341), a pattern associated with poorer external generalization; by contrast PGS002075 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (731,196) and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries, supporting portability. PGS002075 lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only partial-r 0.0385), so confidence is not high, but overall phenotype fidelity plus stronger structural/method signals outweigh the modest PRS-only metric advantage of the sparse framework score.

PGS003381 is better supported for the target “uterine cancer” because its endpoint is the clinically dominant subtype (endometrial carcinoma) and is consistently aligned across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS000541 uses a broader “malignant neoplasm of uterus” label that can mix heterogeneous uterine malignancies. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a PRS metric; however, PGS003381 has a much stronger structural PRS signal (lassosum genome-wide shrinkage with 529,365 variants) than PGS000541’s 18-SNP GWAS-hits score, which is typically weaker for polygenic risk. Covariates are basic in both (age+PCs vs age+sex+PCs/batch), with no obvious leakage. Overall, endpoint fidelity plus markedly stronger method/variant coverage favors PGS003381 despite missing training N.

PGS001536 is better supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only metrics (AUROC 0.64193; R² 0.01621) with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, array, PCs) and has defined training (UKB; n=269,704) plus multi-ancestry evaluation (though selected record is EUR). In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata inconsistency for the target trait: despite trait_reported/EFO being vitiligo, phenotyping_reported is "Red hair" (suggesting phenotype mismatch/contamination), and it lacks PRS-only AUC/R² (only a pseudo R²/full-model-like metric shown). While PGS001536 comes from a pan-trait framework paper (a penalty), the strong phenotype mismatch signal and missing PRS-only metrics in PGS000738 make PGS001536 the more defensible choice overall.

PGS001795 is the better-supported choice for the target trait “uterine cancer” because its endpoint matches the umbrella trait directly (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: “Uterine cancer”; trait_efo: uterine carcinoma) and it reports a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2 / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 = 0.001948), whereas PGS003381 targets the dominant subtype (uterine endometrial carcinoma / endometrial carcinoma) and only provides full-model metrics (AUROC=0.761, R2=0.11) that are not PRS-only and thus not comparable for PRS ranking. Although PGS003381 uses only basic covariates (age, PCs) and has a slightly smaller validation N, the lack of PRS-only performance evidence makes its apparent higher AUROC likely covariate-driven; PGS001795’s explicit PRS-only R2 provides cleaner evidence despite being from a global biobank framework context.

PGS001536 is endpoint-aligned to vitiligo (trait_reported/trait_efo match; phenotyping_reported is vitiligo time-to-event) and reports PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193, PGS-only R2=0.01621), which is plausible under the vitiligo h2_obs ceiling (~0.17). It also has broader evaluation ancestry (AFR/EAS/EUR/SAS) with basic covariates only. In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is anti–PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients (treatment-induced, different endpoint), provides no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only an HR=1.41 and a meta-analysis p-value), and has a very small validation sample (n=1,584) limited to EUR—making it much less supported for generic vitiligo risk.

PGS001795 is the better-supported uterine cancer PRS because it reports a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) with basic covariates and a large external-style evaluation sample (n=170,276) drawn from a multi-biobank global framework, and its R2 is plausible relative to the low uterine-cancer heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0005). In contrast, PGS000541 is a very sparse 18-variant GWAS-hits score and does not provide any explicit PGS-only AUC/R2; the available AUROC=0.576 and pseudo-R2=0.0133 appear to be full-model/unclear comparability metrics, making its PRS signal harder to judge despite reporting ORs. Endpoint alignment is acceptable for both (uterine cancer vs malignant neoplasm of uterus), so the deciding edge is that PGS001795 has cleaner PRS-specific performance reporting and much broader evaluation support than PGS000541.

PGS000738 is better supported for the target trait vitiligo because its endpoint evidence is at least disease-context coherent (publication focused on autoimmune vitiligo/polygenic inheritance) and it provides a PRS-relevant quantitative signal (pseudo R²=0.0386; β=0.695) from a European validation (n=4,702). In contrast, PGS000760 has a clear endpoint mismatch in phenotyping_reported (anti–PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients), which is treatment-induced and thyroid-autoimmunity oriented rather than vitiligo status; its reported metric is a meta-analysis p-value and an HR=1.41 in that therapy-specific context, offering weaker direct evidence for vitiligo risk prediction despite a large training N. Both lack PGS-only AUC/R², so phenotype fidelity dominates; PGS000738 is the closer-supported vitiligo PRS candidate.
